overview.title: 📖 Overview: Tereifot, Their Young, and Two Kinds of Hekdesh
overview.subtitle: Temurah 31a–31b
overview.hebrewSource: יֵשׁ בְּקׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ מַה שֶּׁאֵין בְּקׇדְשֵׁי בֶדֶק הַבַּיִת, וְיֵשׁ בְּקׇדְשֵׁי בֶדֶק הַבַּיִת מַה שֶּׁאֵין בְּקׇדְשֵׁי מִזְבֵּחַ
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the previous chapter's argument over whether the young of a tereifa may be sacrificed, and locates the dispute precisely: it depends on whether a tereifa can conceive at all, and on whether a fetus counts as 'the thigh of its mother'. It then extends the question to a chick hatched from a tereifa hen's egg, and to a kosher animal raised on a tereifa's milk. A new mishna opens the last chapter, setting out a two-column comparison: what is true of animals consecrated for the altar but not of property consecrated for Temple maintenance, and the reverse.

slides.title: 🐣 Where Exactly Do Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis Disagree?
slides.subtitle: The location of the dispute depends on a prior question — can a tereifa give birth?

boxes.title: If a tereifa CAN give birth
items: The case is: became a tereifa first, then conceived
R' Eliezer: this permitted factor (the father) and that prohibited factor (the mother) together → prohibited
The Rabbis: such a combination → permitted, like its father

boxes.title: If a tereifa CANNOT survive to give birth
items: The case is: conceived first, then became a tereifa
R' Eliezer: a fetus is the thigh of its mother — barred exactly as she is
The Rabbis: a fetus is not the thigh of its mother — no reason to bar it

boxes.title: Rav Huna's added claim
items: The Rabbis concede on a chick from a tereifa dove's egg
An animal fetus develops as its own entity in the womb
But an egg grows out of the hen's own body — so the taint carries

callout.label: The move:
callout.text: Rather than choose between the two readings, the Gemara shows each is coherent once you fix the biological premise — a standard way of preserving both traditions.

slides.title: 🪱 Rava's Proof and Abaye's Reversal
slides.subtitle: A baraita about worms is enlisted, then turned around

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: A baraita supports Rav Huna: a ladleful of worms that came from a living person who then died — R' Eliezer says they impart corpse impurity, the Rabbis deem them pure.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: The Rabbis dissent only about worms, which are a mere secretion. About an egg, which is part of the hen's body, even they would concede the chick is barred.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: No — the opposite is more reasonable. R' Eliezer takes worms to be part of the person, since a person is called a worm in his lifetime: 'the hope of man is a worm' (Job 25:6).

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: But a chick emerges only once the egg rots, and what has rotted is mere dust, no longer ascribed to the hen. Even R' Eliezer should permit it.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: And it is taught explicitly in a baraita that R' Eliezer concedes the chick from a tereifa's egg is permitted — against Rav Huna.

callout.label: Outcome:
callout.text: Abaye's explicit baraita is the stronger evidence; Rav Huna's inference from the worms does not hold.

slides.title: 🍼 A Kosher Animal That Suckled From a Tereifa
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus disqualifies it — but on what theory?

nodes.content: ❓ Is it because the animal was simply fattened from a tereifa?
🚫 That cannot be it — otherwise feeding an animal vetches of idolatry would bar it too, and it does not (unless the animal itself was set aside for idolatry)
💡 Rabbi Ḥanina Terita taught before Rabbi Yoḥanan: the case is being given warm, fresh milk every morning
✅ Each suckling sustains it for a full twenty-four hours, so the animal lives entirely off the tereifa — and is therefore disqualified from the altar

callout.label: Distinction:
callout.text: Not nourishment in general, but total dependence for survival, is what transfers the disqualification.

slides.title: 🔪 Why a Tereifa Sacrificial Animal Is Never Redeemed
slides.subtitle: Deriving the limits of benefit from a redeemed disqualified offering
slides.hebrewSource: רַק בְּכׇל אַוַּת נַפְשְׁךָ תִּזְבַּח וְאָכַלְתָּ בָשָׂר בְּכׇל שְׁעָרֶיךָ
slides.label: The rule and its source:
slides.text: The mishna holds that sacrificial animals that became tereifot are not redeemed — one does not redeem consecrated animals merely to feed them to dogs, which degrades them. The Sages read Deuteronomy 12:15, which governs redeemed disqualified offerings: 'you may slaughter' — but you may not shear their wool; 'and eat' — but you may not drink their milk. A second version reads it as a timeline instead: benefit is permitted only from the slaughter onward, so shearing and milk, which belong to the animal's lifetime, are excluded. On that second reading the tanna evidently does allow redeeming a consecrated animal to feed dogs, since that too comes after slaughter.

slides.title: ⚖️ Altar Consecrations vs. Temple Maintenance
slides.subtitle: The opening mishna of the final chapter, set side by side

callout.label: Two clarifications:
callout.text: The 'everything consecrated for the altar makes a substitute' rule was taught only of a principal offering — not of birds, meal offerings, offspring or a substitute itself. And Rabbi Abbahu derives paying craftsmen from maintenance funds from 'And let them make Me a sanctuary' (Ex. 25:8) — it may be built from what is Mine.

summary.principle: A disqualification passes to the next generation only where mother and offspring are treated as one body — and the chapter's new mishna sorts every consecration into altar or Temple maintenance, each with its own set of consequences.

flowSteps.content: 🐣 Offspring of a tereifa: dispute located by whether a tereifa can conceive, and whether a fetus is 'the thigh of its mother'

columns.content: 🥚 Chick from a tereifa's egg: Rav Huna bars it, but an explicit baraita has R' Eliezer permitting
🍼 Suckled on fresh milk daily: barred, because it survives entirely off the tereifa

flowSteps.content: 🔪 'Slaughter and eat' — no wool, no milk from a redeemed disqualified animal; a tereifa offering is not redeemed at all
⚖️ New mishna: altar consecrations make substitutes and carry karet; maintenance consecrations take effect on everything and pay the craftsmen
🎓 Key Principle: an unspecified consecration defaults to Temple maintenance — but Rav holds nobody forfeits an altar-fit animal to maintenance if the herd allows otherwise

quiz.q: According to the view that a tereifa CAN give birth, where do Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disagree?
o: Where the animal conceived first and then became a tereifa
Where the animal became a tereifa first and then conceived
Where the animal was consecrated before becoming a tereifa
Where the offspring itself became a tereifa
quiz.e: On that premise the case is tereifa-then-pregnant, and the dispute is the general rule of 'this permitted factor and that prohibited factor': Rabbi Eliezer bars the result, the Rabbis permit it like its father.

quiz.q: What is Abaye's objection to Rav Huna's ruling about a chick from a tereifa's egg?
o: A hen cannot become a tereifa
A chick emerges only once the egg has rotted, and what has rotted is mere dust no longer ascribed to the hen
Eggs are always permitted since they are not flesh
Rav Huna contradicted his own earlier ruling
quiz.e: Abaye argues the reverse of Rava's reading and adds a decisive point: a baraita explicitly states that Rabbi Eliezer concedes the chick from a tereifa's egg may be sacrificed, contrary to Rav Huna.

quiz.q: Why is a kosher animal that suckled from a tereifa disqualified, according to Rabbi Ḥanina Terita's teaching before Rabbi Yoḥanan?
o: Because any nourishment from a tereifa transfers its status
Because it was given warm milk each morning and so survives entirely on the tereifa for each twenty-four-hour period
Because the milk of a tereifa is itself a sacrificial by-product
Because the animal is presumed to have become a tereifa itself
quiz.e: Mere fattening cannot be the reason — feeding an animal vetches of idolatry does not bar it. The disqualification requires that the animal's continued existence depend on the tereifa.

quiz.q: Which of these is true of animals consecrated for the altar but NOT of property consecrated for Temple maintenance?
o: Unspecified consecrations default to it
One is liable for misuse of its by-products such as milk and eggs
It renders an animal exchanged for it a substitute
The Temple treasurer may pay craftsmen from it
quiz.e: Only altar consecrations generate temurah. The other three options are all features of Temple-maintenance consecrations, which the mishna lists in the opposite column.

quiz.q: From where does Rabbi Abbahu derive that craftsmen may be paid from funds consecrated for Temple maintenance?
o: 'You may slaughter and eat flesh within all your gates' (Deut. 12:15)
'And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them' (Ex. 25:8)
'The hope of man is a worm' (Job 25:6)
'You shall not bring the payment of a prostitute' (Deut. 23:19)
quiz.e: 'And let them make Me a sanctuary' indicates the Tabernacle may be constructed from that which is God's — from consecrated property — so maintenance funds may compensate the workers.
